ShowTime OTT Platform — Linear Regression Analysis¶

Predicting First-Day Content Viewership¶

Author: Shankar Ganesh D Course Project — Linear Regression

Executive Summary¶

Objective. Identify the factors driving first-day content viewership on the ShowTime OTT platform and build a model to forecast first-day views for upcoming releases.

Approach. Multiple linear regression on 1,000 content releases, using platform traffic, advertising impressions, trailer engagement, sporting-event overlap, genre, release day and season as predictors. Fitted on 800 releases and validated on 200 held out.

Model performance. The model explains 77.4% of the variation in first-day viewership on unseen data (training R² = 0.787, test R² = 0.774), with a test-set mean absolute error of 0.0399 million views. All five regression assumptions were tested and satisfied.

Key findings¶

Factor Effect on first-day views Significance
Trailer views +2,311 views per million trailer views p < 0.001
Major sporting event −59,600 views (−12.6% of average) p < 0.001
Saturday vs Friday release +52,600 views (+11.1%) p < 0.001
Wednesday vs Friday release +49,500 views (+10.5%) p < 0.001
Summer vs Fall release +44,600 views (+9.4%) p < 0.001
Platform visitors +12,900 views per million visitors p < 0.001
Advertising impressions No measurable effect p = 0.180
Genre No measurable effect p ≥ 0.14 (all)

Headline conclusion¶

ShowTime releases 37% of its content on Friday — its worst-performing day of the week. Friday averages 0.447 million first-day views against Saturday's 0.498 million and Wednesday's 0.495 million. Rebalancing the release calendar, avoiding sporting-event clashes and favouring Summer release windows together represent an estimated 33% improvement in first-day viewership, with no additional content or marketing spend required.

Meanwhile, advertising impressions — which span a two-fold range across releases — show no detectable relationship with first-day viewership, while trailer engagement emerges as by far the strongest predictor available before a title even launches.

Section 1 — Introduction¶

1.1 Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

ShowTime is an OTT media service provider offering movies, web shows, and other digital content to its users. The platform wants to understand the factors that influence the first-day viewership of newly released content.

The first-day viewership of content can be influenced by several factors, such as the number of visitors to the platform, advertising and promotional activities, trailer engagement, release day, season, genre, and the occurrence of major sporting events.

Business Objective¶

The objective of this analysis is to identify the key factors that influence first-day content viewership and develop a Linear Regression model that can predict the first-day views of content on the ShowTime platform.

Target Variable: views_content

1.2 Key Questions to be Answered¶

The following questions are specified for the EDA section of this project:

  1. What does the distribution of content views look like?
  2. What does the distribution of genres look like?
  3. The day of the week on which content is released generally plays a key role in the viewership. How does the viewership vary with the day of release?
  4. How does the viewership vary with the season of release?
  5. What is the correlation between trailer views and content views?

All variables in the dataset are examined thoroughly in the EDA section beyond these five questions, as instructed, so that every predictor's relationship with viewership — not only the ones named above — is understood before modelling.

1.3 Dataset Overview¶

The dataset contains 1,000 observations and 8 variables related to content releases on the OTT platform. The variables include information about:

  • Platform visitors
  • Advertising impressions
  • Major sports events
  • Content genre
  • Release day
  • Release season
  • Trailer views
  • First-day content views

1.4 Variable Classification¶

Variable Type Description
visitors Numerical Average platform visitors in the past week, in millions
ad_impressions Numerical Advertising impressions for the content, in millions
major_sports_event Categorical/Binary Whether a major sports event occurred on the release day
genre Categorical Genre of the content
dayofweek Categorical Day on which the content was released
season Categorical Season in which the content was released
views_trailer Numerical Trailer views, in millions
views_content Numerical First-day content views, in millions (target)

Answer to Question 1 — What does the distribution of content views look like?

First-day content viewership (views_content) has a mean of 0.473 million views, a median of 0.45 million, and ranges from 0.22 to 0.89 million. The distribution is positively skewed (skewness = 0.94): most releases achieve between roughly 0.35 and 0.55 million views, with a smaller number of releases reaching substantially higher first-day viewership. This right tail represents genuine high-performing content rather than a symmetric spread around the mean.

For context, visitors is mildly skewed (0.37), ad_impressions moderately skewed (1.03), and views_trailer is the most heavily skewed variable in the dataset (2.37) — its distribution is examined further below since it turns out to be the strongest driver of viewership.

Outlier Treatment Decision: The IQR method flags potential outliers in all four numerical variables, with views_trailer the most affected at 18.9% of observations. Inspection of the extreme values shows two distinct patterns: visitors and ad_impressions both have their top-ten values tied at exactly 2.34 and 2,424.20 respectively, indicating the source data is already capped at a ceiling rather than containing runaway errors. views_trailer and views_content decline gradually from their maxima, consistent with a genuine long right tail of high-performing content rather than data errors.

No observations are removed or capped. Removing them would discard exactly the high-viewership releases the business most wants to understand. Whether these observations exert undue influence on the fitted model is checked formally later using Cook's distance (Section 5.7), after the model is built.

Answer to Question 5 — What is the correlation between trailer views and content views?

The Pearson correlation between views_trailer and views_content is 0.754, indicating a strong positive linear relationship — by far the strongest of any numerical predictor examined. Content with higher trailer viewership consistently achieves higher first-day views.

For comparison, visitors correlates at 0.259 (weak positive) and ad_impressions at 0.050 (effectively no linear relationship). Advertising volume, despite spanning more than a two-fold range across releases (1,011 to 2,424 million impressions), shows almost no association with first-day viewership on its own.

Answer to Question 3 — How does viewership vary with the day of release?

Average first-day viewership varies meaningfully across release days. Saturday has the highest mean viewership (0.498 million), closely followed by Wednesday (0.495 million), while Friday has the lowest (0.447 million) — a gap of roughly 0.051 million views, or about 11% of Friday's own mean. Notably, Friday is also the single most-used release day (369 of 1,000 releases), meaning the platform's heaviest release day is its weakest-performing one. Monday and Tuesday show relatively high means but rest on very few observations (24 and 23) and should be interpreted cautiously. This relationship is tested formally, controlling for other factors, in the regression model.

Answer to Question 4 — How does viewership vary with the season of release?

First-day viewership shows a consistent gradient across seasons: Summer is highest (0.497 million), followed by Winter (0.485 million), Spring (0.467 million), and Fall is lowest (0.445 million). Since the four seasons are almost evenly represented (244–257 releases each), this comparison is not distorted by sample-size imbalance, unlike the day-of-week comparison above. The gap between Summer and Fall (0.051 million, ~11%) is comparable in size to the Saturday-vs-Friday gap.

2.8 Summary of EDA Insights¶

  • Target variable: first-day viewership averages 0.473 million views (median 0.45), positively skewed, ranging 0.22–0.89 million.
  • Strongest driver: views_trailer (r = 0.754) — far stronger than visitors (r = 0.259) or ad_impressions (r = 0.050).
  • Advertising volume shows almost no linear relationship with viewership despite a two-fold range across releases.
  • Sporting events depress viewership by roughly 10% on average.
  • Release day is the clearest operational finding: Friday is used most (37% of releases) but performs worst; Saturday and Wednesday perform best.
  • Season shows a consistent gradient: Summer > Winter > Spring > Fall.
  • Genre shows limited separation between categories relative to day/season effects.
  • Numerical predictors are nearly uncorrelated with each other, which is favourable for the regression model that follows.

Section 3 — Data Preprocessing¶

3.1 Feature Engineering¶

Three candidate features are constructed and tested against their raw counterparts. A feature is retained only if there is evidence it improves the model.

Feature Retention Decision¶

log_views_trailer — not retained. The log transform reduces skewness from 2.37 to 1.87 but slightly weakens the correlation with the target (0.751 vs 0.754 raw). Since the untransformed relationship is already strongly linear and later diagnostics show no evidence of non-linearity, the raw variable is kept for interpretability — its coefficient reads directly as "additional first-day views per million trailer views".

ad_per_visitor — not retained. Advertising intensity correlates at −0.099, which is larger in magnitude than raw impressions (0.050) but now negative — more ad exposure relative to platform size is weakly associated with lower viewership. This is more likely a proxy for smaller-audience releases receiving heavier relative promotion than a genuine effect, and it does not offer a cleaner story than the raw variable. Retained as a candidate for follow-up analysis rather than included in the primary model.

is_weekend — not retained. Weekend releases do average higher viewership (0.492 vs 0.470), but the flag would misclassify the most important pattern in the data: Wednesday (0.4946) performs almost identically to the weekend average, while Friday (0.4467) — a weekday — is the worst performer of all. Collapsing seven days into two would erase this distinction. The full day-of-week dummy encoding is retained; the thin Monday/Tuesday samples are flagged as a limitation.

Conclusion: no transformation is applied beyond categorical dummy encoding. The engineered features were constructed and tested; the raw specification is retained because the evidence does not support replacing it.

3.2 Encode Categorical Variables¶

In [30]:
X = df.drop('views_content', axis=1)
y = df['views_content']

categorical_cols = ['genre', 'dayofweek', 'season']
X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=categorical_cols, drop_first=True, dtype=int)

print("Shape after encoding:", X.shape)
print("\nPredictor columns:")

Shape after encoding: (1000, 20)

Predictor columns:
['visitors', 'ad_impressions', 'major_sports_event', 'views_trailer', 'genre_Comedy', 'genre_Drama', 'genre_Horror', 'genre_Others', 'genre_Romance', 'genre_Sci-Fi', 'genre_Thriller', 'dayofweek_Monday', 'dayofweek_Saturday', 'dayofweek_Sunday', 'dayofweek_Thursday', 'dayofweek_Tuesday', 'dayofweek_Wednesday', 'season_Spring', 'season_Summer', 'season_Winter']

drop_first=True was used to avoid the dummy-variable trap. The omitted (reference) category for each variable is: genre → Action, dayofweek → Friday, season → Fall. Every dummy coefficient in the model is interpreted relative to these reference categories.

3.3 Train-Test Split¶

In [31]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42)

5.4 Model Findings: The model explains 78.68% of the variation in first-day viewership on training data (adjusted R² = 78.14%). The overall F-test is significant (p < 0.001). visitors, major_sports_event, and views_trailer are significant numerical/binary predictors; visitors and trailer views are positively associated with viewership, while sports events are negatively associated. All day-of-week and season dummies are significant relative to their Friday and Fall reference categories, all with positive coefficients. ad_impressions and all genre dummies are not statistically significant at the 5% level.

Finding: The partial F-test gives F = 1.021, p = 0.418. Since p > 0.05, the eight dropped coefficients (ad_impressions and the seven genre dummies) are not jointly significant — dropping them costs no explanatory power. The reduced model's adjusted R² (0.7813) is essentially identical to the full model's (0.7814), while both its AIC (−2523.7 vs −2516.0) and BIC (−2462.8 vs −2417.7) are lower, favouring the simpler model on parsimony grounds.

The full model is retained as the primary specification, since it lets the non-significance of advertising and genre be reported explicitly as a business finding. The reduced model confirms this choice costs nothing in fit.

5.1 Linearity¶

    ax.set_title(f'Residuals vs {col}')
plt.tight_layout()

Mean of residuals: 7.80e-14

Finding: The residuals are scattered around zero with no systematic curved pattern, either against fitted values or against each continuous predictor individually. The mean of the residuals is effectively zero (3.8×10⁻¹⁵), as expected for OLS with an intercept. The linearity assumption is reasonably satisfied.

5.2 Independence of Errors¶

In [41]:

Durbin-Watson statistic: 2.038

Finding: The Durbin-Watson statistic (2.038) is close to 2, indicating no evidence of first-order autocorrelation in the residuals. The independence assumption is satisfied.

5.3 Normality of Residuals¶

Finding: The Q-Q plot shows the residuals closely follow the theoretical normal line, with only minor tail deviations. The Shapiro-Wilk p-value (0.4379) exceeds 0.05, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis of normality. The normality assumption is reasonably satisfied.

5.4 Homoscedasticity¶

Finding: The Breusch-Pagan p-value (0.4245) exceeds 0.05, so we fail to reject the null of constant residual variance. There is no significant evidence of heteroscedasticity; the homoscedasticity assumption is reasonably satisfied.

Section 6 — Model Performance Evaluation¶

In [47]:
X_test_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test)
y_train_pred = model.predict(X_train_sm)

def regression_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    mape = np.mean(np.abs((y_true - y_pred) / y_true)) * 100
    r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
    return mae, rmse, mape, r2

train_mae, train_rmse, train_mape, train_r2 = regression_metrics(y_train, y_train_pred)

Finding: The model explains 78.68% of variation on training data and 77.43% on unseen test data — a gap of only 0.0125, indicating the model generalises well rather than overfitting. The test-set mean absolute error is 0.0399 million views and RMSE is 0.0500 million, which is 10.71% of the average viewership (0.473 million). The mean absolute percentage error is 9.08%. RMSE exceeds MAE because it penalises large errors more heavily, but the gap between them is modest — the model has no small set of severely mispredicted releases. In practical terms, a typical release's first-day forecast lands within roughly 40,000 views of the actual figure — precise enough to support scheduling and capacity-planning decisions, though not to forecast an individual release exactly.

Section 7 — Actionable Business Insights and Recommendations¶

7.1 Key Business Insights¶

1. Trailer engagement is the single strongest lever on first-day viewership¶

views_trailer has coefficient 0.002311 (p < 0.001, t = 45.8) — the most significant predictor in the model. Every additional 1 million trailer views is associated with roughly 2,311 additional first-day content views. Across the observed trailer-performance range (30M to 200M views), this accounts for a swing of approximately 0.39 million first-day views — larger than the entire average viewership of 0.473 million.

2. Releasing during a major sporting event costs roughly one-eighth of the audience¶

major_sports_event = −0.059559 (p < 0.001). A release coinciding with a major sporting event loses approximately 59,600 first-day views — 12.6% of average viewership — after controlling for trailer engagement, traffic, genre, and season.

3. ShowTime releases most of its content on its worst-performing day¶

Friday carries 369 of 1,000 releases (37%) and has the lowest mean first-day viewership of any day (0.447 million). Every other day carries a positive, significant coefficient against Friday:

Release day Coefficient vs Friday Additional first-day views Releases in data
Saturday +0.0526 ~52,600 88
Wednesday +0.0495 ~49,500 332
Monday +0.0451 ~45,100 24
Sunday +0.0388 ~38,800 67
Tuesday +0.0324 ~32,400 23
Thursday +0.0196 ~19,600 97
Friday reference — 369

Saturday outperforms Friday by ~52,600 views (11.1% of average), yet is used for only 88 releases. Wednesday performs almost as well and is already used heavily (332 releases), confirming the platform can execute mid-week releases successfully. Caution: Monday and Tuesday rest on only 24 and 23 observations and carry wide confidence intervals — Saturday and Wednesday are the well-supported estimates to act on.

4. Platform traffic contributes a meaningful but smaller effect¶

visitors = 0.128909 (p < 0.001): each additional million weekly platform visitors is associated with ~12,900 additional first-day views. Moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of traffic (1.55M → 1.83M) is worth ~36,100 views, or 7.6% of average viewership.

5. Season produces a consistent gradient, Summer strongest¶

Season Coefficient vs Fall Additional first-day views % of mean
Summer +0.0446 ~44,600 9.4%
Winter +0.0265 ~26,500 5.6%
Spring +0.0232 ~23,200 4.9%
Fall reference — —

6. Advertising volume shows no independent effect¶

ad_impressions is not significant (p = 0.180); raw correlation with viewership is 0.050. Across the observed range (1,011–2,424 million impressions), the model attributes a difference of only ~11,000 views — not statistically distinguishable from zero.

7. Genre does not independently predict first-day viewership¶

None of the seven genre dummies is significant (p ≥ 0.14). Once trailer engagement, timing and traffic are controlled for, genre adds nothing measurable.

Combined effect¶

A release moved from Friday to Saturday (+52,600), scheduled in Summer instead of Fall (+44,600), and kept clear of a major sporting event (+59,600) gains approximately 156,800 first-day views — a 33% improvement over average viewership — with no change to the content itself or the marketing budget.

7.2 Business Recommendations¶

1. Rebalance the release calendar away from Friday — highest priority. Friday absorbs 37% of releases while performing worst. Shift high-value titles toward Saturday and Wednesday; even reallocating 50 releases a year could add ~2.5 million first-day views annually. Validate with a controlled test before restructuring the full calendar, since the Friday concentration may reflect contractual or industry norms not captured here.

2. Screen release dates against the major sporting calendar. A clash costs ~12.6% of first-day viewership and is largely avoidable, since sporting calendars are published well in advance.

3. Use trailer performance as a pre-release forecasting instrument. Trailer views are observable before release and are the strongest predictor available — forecast expected first-day demand at ~2,311 views per million trailer views to support capacity and promotional decisions.

4. Audit advertising effectiveness rather than advertising volume. Impressions show no measurable link to first-day viewership across a two-fold spending range. Investigate targeting, creative, and channel mix; consider redirecting some impression spend toward trailer promotion.

5. Concentrate flagship releases in Summer; support Fall releases more heavily. Summer outperforms Fall by ~9.4% of average viewership.

6. Stop using genre as a demand-planning input. Genre carries no independent predictive power once other factors are controlled for.

Priority Action Est. effect Cost to implement
1 Avoid sporting-event clashes ~59,600 views (12.6%) Minimal
2 Shift Friday releases to Sat/Wed ~50,000 views (10.6%) Low
3 Favour Summer over Fall windows ~44,600 views (9.4%) Low
4 Trailer-based forecasting Operational Medium
5 Advertising effectiveness audit TBD Medium

Section 8 — Final Conclusion¶

8.1 Conclusion¶

The objective of this analysis was to identify the factors associated with first-day content viewership on the ShowTime platform and to develop a model to predict first-day views. A multiple linear regression model using platform visitors, advertising impressions, major sports event status, trailer views, genre, day of week, and season achieved an R² of 0.7868 (adjusted 0.7814) on training data and 0.7743 on unseen test data, with an F-test significant at p < 0.001. visitors, views_trailer, major_sports_event, release day, and season were statistically significant predictors; advertising impressions and genre were not. All five regression assumptions were tested with no material violations: linearity held, Durbin-Watson = 2.038, Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.4379, Breusch-Pagan p = 0.4245, and all VIFs were below 5. Influence diagnostics confirmed no observation exerts outsized leverage on the fit.

8.2 Limitations¶

  • Association, not causation. Releases were not randomly assigned to days, seasons, or sporting-event windows; scheduling may correlate with unobserved factors. Recommendations should be validated with controlled tests before being adopted at scale.
  • Thin support for two release days. Monday (n=24) and Tuesday (n=23) carry wide confidence intervals and should not drive scheduling decisions on their own.
  • Unbalanced release-day distribution. Friday and Wednesday account for ~70% of releases; the Friday finding is well-supported, sparser-day comparisons less so.
  • Omitted variables. Production budget, cast, critical reception, prior-season performance, competing platforms, and audience demographics are not in the dataset and likely explain much of the remaining ~22% of unexplained variation.
  • Single-day outcome. The target measures only first-day viewership; content that builds an audience over subsequent weeks is not captured.
  • Reference-category dependence. All categorical coefficients are relative to Action (genre), Friday (day), and Fall (season).
  • Sporting-event variable is binary. It does not distinguish a major final from a routine fixture.
  • Advertising measured as volume only. The null result should be read as "impression volume does not predict first-day viewership," not "advertising does not work."

8.3 Executive Summary¶

Business Objective: Identify factors associated with first-day content viewership and develop a model to predict first-day views for ShowTime content.

Key Findings:

  • Trailer views show the strongest positive association with first-day viewership (r = 0.754).
  • Platform visitors have a significant positive association.
  • Major sporting events reduce estimated first-day viewership by ~12.6%.
  • Release day and season show significant differences relative to their reference categories — notably, Friday (the most-used day) performs worst.
  • Advertising impressions and genre show no significant independent effect.

Model Performance: Training R² 0.7868 · Adjusted R² 0.7814 · Testing R² 0.7743 · MAE 0.0399 · RMSE 0.0500 · MAPE 9.08%

Model Diagnostics: Linearity satisfied · Independence (DW = 2.038) · Normality (Shapiro p = 0.4379) · Homoscedasticity (BP p = 0.4245) · No problematic multicollinearity (max VIF 2.75) · No high-influence observations (max Cook's D 0.016)

Business Implication: ShowTime can use trailer engagement, platform traffic, release-day timing, seasonal patterns, and the sporting-events calendar as concrete, actionable inputs for release planning and first-day demand forecasting — with rebalancing away from Friday releases as the single highest-leverage, lowest-cost change available.
